transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-21 15:00 PST
Duration: ~55 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jared (Redwood SE), Priya (Redwood SRE); Rachel (CTO), Samir (ML Eng), Lena (Infra), Tom (Benchmarking)

Summary section (auto): quick notes - main ask is get a realistic baseline on Aurora's 8k and 32k prompt sets, compare TensorRT-LLM tuned inference vs vLLM with caching, and validate CUDA graph warm-up patterns end-to-end in Aurora's VPC.

00:00:12 Maya: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Maya with Redwood, Jared's here on the SE side, Priya our SRE. Rachel: Thanks, yeah we booked this to talk scale and perf for the next quarter.
00:00:28 Jared: Quick agenda - kernel selection and heuristics, TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM results we've seen, cudagraphs patterns, kv-cache behavior, and then infra/VPC notes. We'll leave time for Q&A and next steps.
00:00:42 Rachel: Sounds good, Samir will run the workloads and Tom will collate.
00:00:55 Samir: Quick context - production is currently generation for analytics summarization, 8k average prompt, some longer 32k retros. Latency target 300ms tail for 8k-ish completions; throughput target 100 qps for batch workloads. We're evaluating hosted vs dedicated vs on-prem.
00:01:18 Jared: Good. On kernel selection - our runtime picks kernels based on model architecture and sequence length distribution. For 8k use-cases we bias towards fused-attention kernels that reduce memory traffic; for 32k we often switch to tiled attention kernels that stream KV more efficiently. This is heuristic-driven and we can override during profiling.
00:01:47 Lena: When you say fused-attention kernels, do you mean the ones that do attention and softmax in a single pass - any tradeoffs for quantized models?
00:01:58 Jared: Exactly. Fused kernels save memory and calls but are sensitive to quantization. For int8 we sometimes see larger accuracy drift unless we use per-channel calibration. fp16 fused kernels are stable.
00:02:15 Tom: We've got strict accuracy constraints - can't exceed 0.5% change in extractive stats.
00:02:22 Priya: Right, so our recommendation is to profile fp16 first with fused kernels, then test int8 with a calibration pass and A/B a prompt set. Jared will share calibration scripts.
00:02:37 Rachel: How do cudagraphs fit in - we've heard mixed guidance on cudagraphs for variable-length workloads.
00:02:45 Jared: Yeah cudagraphs give big wins for stable call patterns - if your token lengths and batch sizes are predictable you can prebuild graphs and save kernel launch overhead; we typically get 15-40% p95 latency improvements in steady-state. For highly variable sequences you either maintain several graphs for different shapes or fall back to dynamic paths. The maintenance complexity is the tradeoff.
00:03:11 Samir: For our summarization jobs, tokens per request vary a lot - 600 to 6k sometimes. Building many graphs seems cumbersome.
00:03:22 Jared: Two practical patterns: 1) build graphs for common prefixes and common batch sizes, then fallback for tail cases; 2) use lightweight warm-up runs that populate the cache and reuse graphs for subsequent similar calls. That second approach reduces the number of graphs needed.
00:03:45 Lena: What's the warm-up cost? If we spin up nodes in our VPC, will cold starts kill the latency SLO?
00:03:52 Priya: Cold start costs are real - on a cold GPU node first few prompts will pay warm-up overhead for cudagraphs and kernel selection. For Dedicated we keep a small warm pool; for on-prem you'd run a lightweight pre-warm pipeline in your bootstrap. Tail latency SLOs require either warm pool or fast fallback policies.
00:04:12 Rachel: Ok. Tell us about vLLM vs TensorRT-LLM differences - we'd like to know which is 'better' for our workloads.
00:04:20 Jared: They're different stacks. TensorRT-LLM is highly optimized for NVIDIA hardware and mixes kernel-level fusion, TensorRT kernels, and aggressive memory planning; it tends to have better absolute throughput especially for larger batch sizes and when using cudagraphs. vLLM is more flexible, lighter-weight, and has excellent KV cache sharing behavior and dynamic batching primitives. In practice: TensorRT wins on throughput/efficiency for fp16/int8 with careful tuning; vLLM often gives better latency for single-stream and for workloads where KV cache reuse across requests matters.
00:05:02 Samir: Any examples with numbers?
00:05:06 Jared: On a T4/RTX A100 class equip - example numbers are rough: TensorRT-LLM + cudagraphs + fp16 might give 4500 tokens/s steady-state on a particular 7B model with batch 8, while vLLM tuned might give 3200 tokens/s but lower tail latency for single client flows. With int8, TensorRT can push higher tokens/s but you'll need calibration and careful validation. These are illustrative; we'll run your same model and prompt set for apples-to-apples.
00:05:40 Tom: And what about kernel selection affecting memory footprint?
00:05:44 Jared: Fused kernels tend to use less intermediate memory but sometimes allocate larger workspace for int8 conversions. Tiled kernels stream KV and keep peak GPU memory lower for long sequences; that's why 32k workloads favor tiled kernels.
00:06:02 Lena: If we go Dedicated or on-prem, are there differences in what we can run? Any driver/HW dependencies?
00:06:10 Priya: For Dedicated we manage drivers and can ensure NVIDIA driver, CUDA, cuDNN, and TensorRT versions are pinned. On-prem you control that matrix; we provide a compatibility matrix and recomended AMI/container images. Some kernels require newer CUDA or specific cuBLAS versions. We'll send the exact matrix.
00:06:30 Rachel: Security/regulatory question - can the KV cache be persisted on disk in our VPC? We want to control retention.
00:06:39 Maya: Yes, for Private deployments KV cache persistence can be controlled; we usually keep in-memory with optional encrypted checkpointing to customer-managed S3/KMS for long-term reuse. Audit logs are all available. We'll include the SOC2 appendix.
00:06:56 Samir: On batching - we want to hit 100 qps but with 300ms p95. We're worried batching to improve throughput will break latency.
00:07:06 Jared: Typical approach is multi-tier routing: low-latency queue routes to a hot path (single or micro-batch) while throughput queue goes through batched workers. You can also autoscale to increase parallelism during peak and use caching to reduce tokens generated. There's always a tradeoff; our console gives token-level latency/cost breakdown to tune that.
00:07:32 Rachel: About quantization - how much quality loss should we expect on our summarization tasks with int8?
00:07:39 Jared: It depends on model family and calibration method. For Llama-like families we often see <1% metric drop with per-channel calibration and KL-based optim; worst case could be 2-3% on sensitive extractive metrics. We recommend an eval set and a canary rollout.
00:07:58 Samir: Can Redwood automate rollouts?
00:08:02 Maya: Yes - we support canary rollouts and automatic rollback on quality regression thresholds tied to your eval set. We'll set that up in the next phase.
00:08:12 Tom: For CUDA graphs - are there gotchas around dynamic shapes and mixed precision?
00:08:18 Jared: Mixed precision is fine, but if you mix int8 conversion kernels inside a graph you must ensure calibration completes first. Dynamic shapes need either shape polymorphism in the graph or multiple graphs. Also note some third-party kernels we use have different graph semantics, so you must test for deterministic correctness.
00:08:40 Samir: For our 32k workloads, what pattern for KV eviction and checkpointing do you recommend?
00:08:46 Jared: For long sequences you should stream KV to host pinned memory and checkpoint every N tokens when idle; keep a sliding window in GPU and prune older KV entries. If you have repeated prefix patterns (e.g., system prompt + few docs) persist those prefixes in a prefix cache to avoid recompute.
00:09:05 Lena: How does network egress factor when running in our VPC and fetching S3 checkpoints?
00:09:11 Priya: If S3 is in VPC, you can use VPC endpoints; egress costs only if crossing regions. We recommend colocating S3 and compute in same AZ/region and using signed pre-signed URLs for uploads. We also support customer-managed KMS for the S3 objects.
00:09:30 Rachel: Cool. Let's talk about the profiling instrumentation you need from us.
00:09:36 Jared: Ideal is: model artifact, example prompt set (8k and 32k), a Dockerfile or container spec of your infra, and perf traces (nvprof / Nsight) if you can capture them. We'll provide a benchmarking harness that runs your prompt permutations and logs per-token latency, kernel timelines, and memory watermarks.
00:09:56 Tom: We can collect Nsight traces in the next cluster run, yeah.
00:10:01 Maya: We'll share the benchmark spreadsheet and a perf-upload endpoint, and Jared will provide baseline scripts.
00:10:10 Samir: On the topic of kernels, any risks of vendor lock-in if we optimize heavily for TensorRT kernels?
00:10:19 Jared: There is some lock-in at the kernel layer; highly-tuned TensorRT kernels may not behave the same on other runtimes. We mitigate this by supporting both TensorRT and vLLM paths and by shipping model variants pinned to runtime. If you want portability, lean on vLLM and keep kernel-optimized paths as optional performance tiers.
00:10:41 Rachel: What about monitoring and alerts for regressions?
00:10:44 Priya: Our console supports token-level latency histograms, model-level quality regression alerts tied to test prompts, and trace linking to cudagraph build times and kernel selection events. We'll show a dashboard in the follow-up.
00:10:58 Tom: Any sample results you can share now?
00:11:03 Jared: We have a sample run on a 13B-ish model: fp16 + cudagraphs gave 22ms per-token p50, int8 baseline 15ms p50 but with a 1.2% metric drop on an extractive test. vLLM single-session p95 was 28ms but with much lower warm-start penalty. These are portfolio numbers not yours. We'll run yours asap.
00:11:28 Rachel: Okay that's helpful.
00:11:32 Maya: Let's sketch the experiment plan: 1) Run fp16 TensorRT-LLM + cudagraphs baseline, 2) Run int8 TensorRT-LLM with per-channel calibration, 3) Run vLLM optimized baseline with dynamic batching and KV cache warm. Each with both 8k and 32k prompt sets.
00:11:56 Samir: How long will runs take? We have a limited cluster window.
00:12:00 Jared: Each permutation for full statistical confidence ~2-3 hours per node; we can parallelize across nodes. If you give us a 24-hour window we can produce stable numbers.
00:12:11 Lena: Any config changes needed on our end for CUDA graph builds?
00:12:14 Jared: Ensure latest drivers and set GPU persistent mode; also allow pinned host memory and increase ulimit for pinned pages if running many processes. We'll send a checklist.
00:12:28 Rachel: Good. A few micro-questions - does Redwood support heterogeneous GPU pools? We sometimes want A100 for heavy batch jobs and A10 for cheaper throughput.
00:12:37 Maya: Yes, Redwood Dedicated can route by GPU class and cost tier. The routing policy can be model-aware. You can also set fallbacks so a cheaper GPU can serve degraded models when A100s are saturated.
00:12:54 Tom: For canarying int8 - what's the recommended rollout percentage?
00:12:58 Priya: Start small, like 2-5% traffic, then 20%, check your eval metrics, then 50%. Use automated rollback if metric thresholds hit.
00:13:08 Samir: Anything else we should watch for?
00:13:10 Jared: Watch memory fragmentation on long-running processes; periodic restart windows help reclaim memory when using aggressive caching. Also monitor kernel-launch variance which can indicate kernel-choice oscillations.
00:13:25 Rachel: Great. Let's open up for quick Q&A on the infra specifics.
00:13:30 Lena: Can you share the compatibility matrix and exact driver versions?
00:13:34 Maya: We'll include it in the follow-up doc.
00:13:40 Tom: Will Redwood's console ingest our Nsight traces or do we need to pre-process?
00:13:45 Jared: We have an ingestion pipeline for Nsight and nvprof traces; we'll annotate them with kernel selectors and build times. You can upload raw traces to the perf endpoint.
00:13:58 Samir: If we see quality drift on int8, what's the quick mitigation?
00:14:03 Jared: Roll back to fp16 for that model and run a more granular calibration set. Also you can do hybrid - keep embedding layers fp16 and quantize transformer blocks.
00:14:15 Rachel: That sounds sensible.
00:14:20 Maya: We're near the end of time so quick recap and next steps?
00:14:25 Jared: Recap: we'll run three baseline permutations with your 8k/32k sets, instrument with Nsight, and share kernel-level timelines. We'll test cudagraphs build strategies and report warm/cold behavior.
00:14:38 Maya: Action items - see the sheet. We'll send the perf upload link and the security checklist. Samir will coordinate cluster windows.
00:14:47 Rachel: Thanks all.
00:14:49 Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with dates.
